items.title: 67559_Art Hodes oral history interview
items.q: The white audience was the Wayne King audience, what we have now, the Lawrence Welk audience

ctx.x: Jimmy Ross' Tavern was on 6th Avenue, and I think either 51st or 50th. But it was right there, not too far from everything, all the happenings. But the people who did find us was the aficionados that were hovering around the jazz movement. There was a great jazz movement in New York at that time. Kids from Columbia University -- Gene Williams, Ralph Gleason, George Avakian was around, I can name so many more that don't come to mind right now. But the whole movement was happening right then. They discovered jazz.…

There was a magazine called Jazz Information, and I was enthralled with this, that there was people that were so crazy about this music. Because that never happened in Chicago. The only -- you see, the blacks had their people to play for, but the whites didn't have it. The white audience was the Wayne King audience, what we have now, the Lawrence Welk audience, is what we had then, in the Wayne King audience.

If you played jazz, you were persona non grata. And if you played your music at night on that Victrola, you better turn it down real soft, and even use a pin for a needle, because if it got too loud, the neighbors would call the law, that noise, they couldn't stand that noise.
